messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Meera is a 67-year-old South Asian woman who has worked for a non-profit organization that provides legal aid to immigrant families for the past two decades. She is married and has two adult children. Seven months ago, while leaving her office late one evening, a man grabbed her from behind in the parking lot, forced her into the back of a van, and sexually assaulted her over the course of several hours before releasing her on a deserted street. She did not report the assault to the police, overwhelmed by a sense of shame and a deep, unshakable belief that she had somehow invited it by working late, by wearing a certain shade of lipstick, by being a woman alone in a city after dark. The event itself was fragmented in her memory—she could recall the cold metal of the van floor against her cheek, the smell of stale cigarettes and sweat, the sound of her own voice pleading—but the story she told herself about it had become solid and unforgiving: she was marked now, permanently damaged, and everyone could see it.

In the weeks that followed, Meera began to avoid the parking lot where it happened, taking a circuitous route through a neighboring alley that added fifteen minutes to her walk. She stopped staying late at work, declining urgent cases that required evening hours, and her supervisor noticed a drop in her productivity. She had always been the reliable one, the staff member who could be counted on to see a case through, but now she left promptly at five, her desk cleared, her eyes fixed on the door. At home, she stopped sitting with her back to the room. She arranged the living room furniture so that she could see the front door from every seat, and she began locking the bedroom door at night, something she had never done in forty years of marriage. Her husband, Raj, asked her what was wrong, and she told him she was just tired, just stressed, just getting older. She could not bring herself to tell him what had happened, because that would mean saying it out loud, and saying it out loud would make it real in a way she could not undo.

She found herself scanning the parking lot every time she left the building, her eyes darting to the shadows between cars, to the open doors of delivery trucks, to the face of every man who walked too close. She was certain that the man who had hurt her was still out there, watching, waiting for her to make another mistake. She became hypervigilant, her heart racing at the sound of a car door slamming, at the sight of a van idling at a stoplight, at the scent of cigarette smoke carried on the wind. She started taking a different route home each day, varying her schedule, never letting herself fall into a pattern that could be predicted. She knew, on some level, that this was exhausting, but she was certain that if she stopped, something terrible would happen again.

What frightened her most, though, was not the memory of the assault itself, but the feeling that she had become someone else. She had always thought of herself as capable, as someone who could handle difficulty. Now she saw herself as weak, as a victim, as a woman who had failed to protect herself. She avoided mirrors, because the face that looked back at her seemed like a stranger's. She stopped wearing the lipstick she had worn that night, throwing it in the trash. She began to believe that she was fundamentally different from other people now, that she carried something invisible but contagious, and that if anyone knew the truth about her, they would recoil. This belief kept her isolated, kept her silent, kept her trapped in a loop of self-blame and fear.

The turning point came when she was assigned a new case: a young woman who had been assaulted by her partner but was too frightened to testify. Meera sat across from her in the intake room, listening to her story, and felt a crack open in the wall she had built around herself. The woman looked at her and said, "You understand, don't you? I can see it in your eyes." Meera nodded, unable to speak, and for the first time in seven months, she allowed herself to cry. She went home that night and told Raj everything, her voice shaking, her hands trembling. He held her, and she felt the shame loosen, just slightly, like a knot beginning to give. The next morning, she called her doctor and asked for a referral to a therapist who specialized in trauma. She is terrified of what she will find when she starts talking about it, but she is more terrified of staying silent. She hopes, more than anything, that she can find a way back to the person she used to be.
